guard_patterns.handling: Require a directly accessible DESNZ or NAEI official source surface for every package.
Keep source-basis, end-user, territorial and residence concepts distinct.
Keep UK, region, local authority, road link, point source, 1x1 km model and parcel levels distinct.
Preserve publication year, inventory year and provisional/final status.
Keep directly located point sources separate from residual or proxy-modelled area sources.
Retain stated modelling limitations and uncertainty differences.
Keep sector definitions, exclusions and reallocations explicit.
Do not silently convert national/local totals, shares or model cells into another aggregation level.
Do not infer a parcel emission value without separate parcel geometry and attribution evidence.
Require deterministic PASS review for structure, provenance, scope and non-parcel semantics.

packages.title: DESNZ nationally consistent local-emissions evidence and use limits QA
facts: The 2005 to 2024 local and regional series is designed as a nationally consistent evidence base for sub-national greenhouse gas emissions.
The local series maintains a consistent time series back to 2005.
The technical report describes local estimates as a spatial disaggregation of the UK Greenhouse Gas Inventory on an end-user basis.
Local estimates are intended to help identify high-emitting sources and energy-intensive sectors.
Local estimates can be used to monitor changes in greenhouse gas emissions over time.
Local estimates can support design and targeting of emissions-reduction strategies.
The local-statistics collection warns that these estimates alone cannot provide all information needed to plan and monitor every local emissions-reduction initiative.
Regional-level results are described as more robust than local-authority results because allocation difficulties have less impact at the larger geography.
Interpretation issues can arise where economic activity or transport crosses local-authority boundaries.
These local-authority estimates are evidence inputs and are not direct measurements of emissions for individual land parcels.

packages.title: DESNZ major-road AADF and road-link mapping QA
facts: The road-emissions mapping uses Ordnance Survey Open Roads for roads in Great Britain.
Major-road traffic-flow data for A-roads and motorways use census count points.
Traffic counts are represented as Annual Average Daily Flow values.
Annual Average Daily Flow values are expanded to annual flows by multiplying by 365.
Expansion factors are used to account for seasonal variation in single-day traffic counts.
Traffic-flow data are separated by vehicle type where source data permit.
Automated allocation of traffic flows to road sections is followed by manual checking and verification.
Vehicle-kilometre estimates for road links are combined with fuel-consumption or emission factors.
Road links are split where they cross local-authority boundaries so estimates can be aggregated by local authority.
Road-link estimates support local-authority attribution but do not establish emissions for a specific land parcel adjacent to the road.

packages.title: DESNZ minor-road model and uncertainty QA
facts: Link-by-link traffic-flow data are not available for most minor roads.
Where direct minor-road flow data are available, they are used to improve mapping accuracy.
Most minor-road traffic flows are modelled from regional average flows and fleet mix.
Regional average flows are applied by minor-road type, including B and C roads and unclassified roads.
The methodology assumes a 30 mph speed limit for urban minor roads where direct speed data are not used.
The methodology assumes a 60 mph speed limit for rural minor roads where direct speed data are not used.
Minor-road calculations are performed at 1 by 1 kilometre resolution before aggregation to local-authority boundaries.
The technical report assigns substantially higher mapping uncertainty to minor roads than to A-roads and motorways.
The report attributes the higher minor-road uncertainty to insufficient traffic-movement measurements for detailed link-level modelling.
A modelled 1 by 1 kilometre minor-road cell must not be represented as a measured parcel-level emission value.

packages.title: NAEI point-source regulatory and reporting-input QA
facts: NAEI defines a point source as an emissions source at a known location with grid references that can be mapped directly.
NAEI receives detailed source data for industrial and commercial point sources.
Point-source inputs include environmental-regulator pollution inventories.
Point-source inputs include installations participating in the EU ETS or UK ETS.
Point-source inputs can also come directly from process operators or trade associations.
Some locally regulated point sources use site-specific information collected from regulators and modelled estimates.
Some point-source emissions are modelled by distributing national estimates over known sources using capacity or another surrogate statistic.
The DESNZ local technical report maps large industrial installations using the NAEI point-source database.
Point-source records can provide strong location evidence while still varying in how emissions are measured, reported or modelled.
A point-source coordinate does not by itself prove cadastral parcel ownership or parcel-boundary containment.

packages.title: NAEI point-source versus residual area-source boundary QA
facts: For some sectors, mapped point sources collectively account for the full national sector total.
For other sectors, point-source datasets cover only the larger reporting installations.
When point-source records cover only part of a sector total, residual emissions remain after the mapped installations are accounted for.
NAEI maps such residual emissions as area sources rather than inventing additional point sources.
Combustion in industry is an example where only larger plants may be represented as reporting point sources.
Coal-fired power stations are given as an example of a sector that can be dominated by mandatory facility reporting.
Point-source and area-source evidence therefore have different spatial precision and should remain distinct.
Residual area-source modelling is not evidence that every grid cell contains a physical emitting installation.
Source-type classification is needed before comparing a mapped point value with a local-authority total.
Neither an area-source residual nor a point-source coordinate can be converted automatically into a parcel value without separate parcel binding.

packages.title: DESNZ local-emissions uncertainty propagation QA
facts: The technical report estimates overall 2024 local-emissions uncertainty using a sum-of-squares approach for propagating component errors.
Sector-specific uncertainty differs according to the quality and spatial resolution of the underlying activity data.
LULUCF net-emission uncertainty is excluded from the main combined uncertainty analysis because it can dominate other components.
The technical report notes local authorities where including LULUCF can at least double total uncertainty.
The report notes several local authorities where including LULUCF can at least triple total uncertainty.
The report identifies an extreme local-authority case where LULUCF can raise uncertainty by about an order of magnitude.
Road-transport uncertainty reflects use of sample or survey data and average flows and speeds.
Minor-road uncertainty is higher because regional-average flows are used where detailed measurements are unavailable.
Smaller industrial, commercial and public-sector fuel distributions can have higher uncertainty where local fuel-use distributions are poorly known.
Published local-level uncertainty must remain attached to its methodology and must not be converted into an unsupported parcel confidence score.

packages.title: DESNZ local-authority gas scope and exclusion QA
facts: The 2005 to 2024 local-authority statistics cover carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide.
Fluorinated gases are excluded from the local-authority statistics because suitable local allocation data are unavailable.
The statistical release states that fluorinated gases represented about 2 percent of UK-level territorial emissions in 2024.
Local statistics exclude aviation, shipping and military transport where there is no obvious basis for allocation to local areas.
The local series is primarily territorial but uses end-user allocation for energy-supply emissions.
Waste emissions are distributed according to where the waste arose rather than simply where landfill emissions physically occur.
Biogenic carbon dioxide from combustion of biofuels is excluded from the reported totals in line with inventory reporting rules.
Non-carbon-dioxide greenhouse gases from biofuel combustion remain included.
Scope differences mean local-authority totals should not be expected to equal every national or residence-basis emissions series.
Scope exclusions must be preserved when using local-authority evidence as a candidate input for later parcel attribution.

packages.title: DESNZ 2024 local-authority sector-share and trend QA
facts: Between 2023 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions decreased in 255 of 361 UK local-authority areas.
That represents 71 percent of local-authority areas in the statistical release.
In 2024, transport accounted for 32 percent of emissions assigned to local-authority areas.
In 2024, the domestic sector accounted for 22 percent of emissions assigned to local-authority areas.
In 2024, industry accounted for 14 percent of emissions assigned to local-authority areas.
In 2024, agriculture accounted for 14 percent of emissions assigned to local-authority areas.
In 2024, the commercial sector accounted for 8 percent of emissions assigned to local-authority areas.
The remaining share came from waste, public-sector and LULUCF categories.
The statistical release says sector dominance varies strongly between local-authority areas because of economic and geographic differences.
National or local-authority sector shares are prioritisation evidence only and are not parcel-specific measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ provisional 2025 national-version guard QA
facts: DESNZ published provisional UK territorial greenhouse gas emissions for 2025 on 2 April 2026.
Total UK net territorial greenhouse gas emissions for 2025 were provisionally estimated at about 367 MtCO2e.
The provisional 2025 estimate was about 2 percent lower than 2024.
Domestic transport was provisionally the largest TES sector in 2025 at 31 percent of net emissions.
Buildings and product uses represented 22 percent of provisional 2025 net emissions.
Agriculture represented 13 percent and industry 11 percent of provisional 2025 net emissions.
The provisional release states that 2025 estimates are subject to revision when final estimates are published.
Data for 1990 to 2024 in the provisional release are consistent with the 2024 final publication.
The provisional methodology does not use the same full process as the final annual inventory for all components.
Provisional national values must not overwrite final 2024 local-authority evidence or be presented as parcel-level 2025 measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ final 2024 source, end-user and SIC basis guard QA
facts: The final 1990 to 2024 DESNZ publication provides UK territorial greenhouse gas emissions.
Final estimates supersede earlier editions after methodological improvements and new data are incorporated.
Source-basis reporting attributes emissions to the sector that directly emits them.
End-user reporting reallocates energy-supply emissions to the users of the energy.
The end-user reallocation is based on modelling rather than direct observation at every consuming location.
DESNZ publishes source estimates first and subsequently adds end-user and SIC views on its publication schedule.
The June 2026 update added the 2024 Standard Industrial Classification emissions annex and dataset.
Source-basis, end-user and SIC outputs answer different analytical questions and cannot be mixed without preserving their basis.
Final national statistics are higher-level evidence than local-authority spatial disaggregation.
No national source, end-user or SIC table alone provides a measured greenhouse gas value for an individual parcel.
